guide.title: Ostia Antica, Rome: the excavated port town, the Museo Ostiense and the castle on Piazza della Rocca
guide.intro: Ostia Antica is a zona of Rome, the thirty-fifth in the city's toponymic series, and it lies in Municipio Roma X at the mouth of the Tiber. Two separate places fill it. The first is the excavated Roman town, about sixty-nine hectares walled in the middle of the first century BC and entered from one ticket office at Viale dei Romagnoli 717: streets of apartment blocks, warehouses, baths, a theatre, a synagogue and mithraea, with a state museum in a former salt store among them. The second is a small brick borgo on Piazza della Rocca, the citadel Pope Gregory IV made out of the medieval settlement, rebuilt in the fifteenth century around a triangular castle, a cathedral and three rows of terraced houses that are still lived in. The zona runs several kilometres, so every place here carries a street.

sections.heading: The excavated town, its ticket and its hours
sections.body:
The Parco archeologico di Ostia antica is an autonomous institute of the Ministero della cultura, created on 23 January 2016 and directed by Alessandro D'Alessio since 30 October 2020. It runs the excavations, the Museo Ostiense inside them, the Castello di Giulio II in the borgo, the riverside quay area at the Saline, and further sites in the Comune di Fiumicino, which is a different comune.

The operator's own page gives the excavations as open Tuesday to Sunday and on public holidays, opening at 08.30 and closing at 16.30 from 25 October to the end of February, 17.15 from 1 to 31 March, 19.00 from 1 April to 30 September and 18.30 from 1 to 24 October. Last entry is one hour before closing and the ticket office shuts an hour before as well. Closed Mondays and 25 December. The integrated ticket is 18.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced for EU citizens aged 18 to 25, valid for eight consecutive days across all the institute's sites, and entry is free on the first Sunday of the month. Audio guides are 7.00 euro for the long route and 5.00 euro for the short route and for children. Guided visits are run by the concessionaire CoopCulture.

The Museo Ostiense keeps its own hours inside those: Tuesday to Sunday, opening at 09.30 from 1 April to 24 October and at 10.30 from 25 October to 31 March, and always closed on the free first Sunday of the month and on the other ministry free days, 25 April, 2 June and 4 November. The Castello di Giulio II is ticketed separately at 6.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced, and is also covered by the 18.00 euro integrated ticket. One part of the site is shut: the operator states that the Necropoli Laurentina is closed to the public for maintenance and restoration.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a station or a bus route for this zona, so none is given here. Steer by addresses instead, and note that the excavations and the borgo are two different destinations with two different doors.

The excavations, the Museo Ostiense and the park's ticket office are at Viale dei Romagnoli 717, 00119 Roma. The operator publishes a telephone line on +39 06 5635801, answered daily from 09.00 to 17.30; the Ministero della cultura lists +39 06 56358099 for the same institute.

The Castello di Giulio II, the basilica of Sant'Aurea and the terraced houses of the borgo stand together on Piazza della Rocca. The operator gives the castle's postal address as Viale dei Romagnoli 717, while Roma Capitale gives Piazza della Rocca; in a zona several kilometres across, the square is the locator worth having, and the basilica's own parish gives Piazza della Rocca 13. The Parco dei Ravennati lies between via dei Martiri Ostiensi, via della Gente Salinatoria, via del Mare, viale dei Romagnoli, via Gesualdo and via Gloriano. The archaeological and naturalistic area of the Saline, with the Roman quay, is reached from viale dei Romagnoli by via delle Saline.

Inside the excavations the monuments are addressed by their ancient streets rather than by numbers: the Decumano Massimo and the Cardo Massimo cross at the Forum, Via di Diana runs past the Casa di Diana and the Thermopolium, Via della Forica leads to the later entrance of the Terme del Foro, and Via delle Tombe runs out of Porta Romana through the necropolis.

sections.heading: The borgo on Piazza della Rocca
sections.body:
The medieval and Renaissance settlement is a second cluster, unconnected to the excavations except by the road between them. From late antiquity the area held the Christian community's cemetery, on the site where tradition placed the tombs of martyrs, among them Santa Aurea. Pope Gregory IV, who reigned from 827 to 844, turned the settlement into a fortified citadel and gave it his name, Gregoriopoli. Martin V had a round tower with a moat built to watch the Tiber; it.wikipedia dates that tower to 1423 and 1424.

Cardinal Guillaume d'Estouteville, bishop of Ostia from 1461 to 1483, restored the Gregoriopoli walls and built three rows of terraced houses inside them, which are still lived in. The year 1483 is the hinge of the borgo's calendar: work began on the fortress, at the expense of Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, later Julius II, and the basilica of Sant'Aurea was finished. Baccio Pontelli is named as the architect of both, and the castle was completed in 1486.

The borgo emptied after the siege by the Duke of Alba in 1556 and the flood of 1557, which diverted the Tiber away from the town and left malarial marshes behind it. The rocca and the borgo were restored in stages during the twentieth century. Twelve bishops of Ostia have been elected pope, and the see's cardinalatial title has been held since the twelfth century by the Dean of the College of Cardinals.

faq.question: What does the ticket cover, and how long is it valid?
faq.answer: The integrated ticket is 18.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced for EU citizens aged 18 to 25, and the operator states that it is valid for eight consecutive days across all the sites of the Parco archeologico di Ostia antica. That includes the excavations, the Museo Ostiense and the Castello di Giulio II, and it also includes sites the institute administers in the Comune di Fiumicino, which is outside Rome. Entry is free on the first Sunday of the month. The castle can also be entered on its own ticket, 6.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced. Audio guides are 7.00 euro for the long route and 5.00 euro for the short route and for children, and guided visits are run by CoopCulture.

faq.question: When are the excavations open?
faq.answer: Tuesday to Sunday and on public holidays, opening at 08.30. Closing time changes four times a year: 16.30 from 25 October to the end of February, 17.15 from 1 to 31 March, 19.00 from 1 April to 30 September and 18.30 from 1 to 24 October. Last entry is one hour before closing and the ticket office closes an hour before as well. The site is closed on Mondays and on 25 December.

faq.question: Is the Museo Ostiense open, and what is in it?
faq.answer: It is open, Tuesday to Sunday, from 09.30 between 1 April and 24 October and from 10.30 between 25 October and 31 March. It is always closed on the free first Sunday of the month and on the other ministry free days, 25 April, 2 June and 4 November. The museum occupies the Casone del Sale inside the excavations and shows the finds in twelve rooms on seven themes, among them the Vittoria Alata from the attic of Porta Romana, the statue of Cartilio Poplicola, fragments of the Fasti Ostienses, the group of Mithras killing the bull signed by the Athenian artist Kriton, the statue of Trajan from the Schola del Traiano and the Sarcofago delle Muse.

faq.question: Is anything here closed to visitors?
faq.answer: Yes. The operator states that the Necropoli Laurentina is closed to the public for maintenance and restoration work. Restoration, consolidation and enhancement works are also under way at the Castello di Giulio II, and there the operator states that the castle stays open on its usual hours, with panels explaining the work. The castle is showing the exhibition IN HOC SIGNO. Testimonianze cristiane tra Ostia e Porto until 21 November 2026.

faq.question: Is Ostia Antica the same as the seaside at Ostia?
faq.answer: No. Ostia Antica is Z. XXXV, a zona at the mouth of the Tiber holding the excavated Roman town and the borgo on Piazza della Rocca. The seafront belongs to the marine quartieri, which are separate units and are written elsewhere in this series. The ancient town was a river port rather than a beach resort: the park's own account records that the Tiber ran along the north side of the town until the flood of 1557 changed its course, and that the coastline is now about four kilometres away.

faq.question: How old is the town, and why was it abandoned?
faq.answer: The park's own account takes the name from ostium, mouth, and records the tradition that Ancus Marcius founded the town in 620 BC to work the salt pans, while the remains identified on the ground begin with the tufa-block castrum of the second half of the fourth century BC. Walls of about the middle of the first century BC enclosed roughly sixty-nine hectares behind three gates, and population estimates for the second century AD run to around fifty thousand. Commerce moved to Portus from the middle of the third century AD, and literary sources describe the town as abandoned by the middle of the sixth.

places.name: Parco archeologico di Ostia antica (Scavi di Ostia)
places.summary: The excavated Roman town at the mouth of the Tiber, entered from the ticket office at Viale dei Romagnoli 717. The operator gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday and public holidays, opening 08.30, closing 16.30 from 25 October to the end of February, 17.15 from 1 to 31 March, 19.00 from 1 April to 30 September and 18.30 from 1 to 24 October, with last entry and ticket sales ending an hour before closing; closed Mondays and 25 December. The integrated ticket is 18.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced for EU citizens aged 18 to 25, valid eight consecutive days across all the institute's sites, and entry is free on the first Sunday of the month. Audio guides are 7.00 euro long route, 5.00 euro short route and 5.00 euro for children; guided visits are run by the concessionaire CoopCulture. Telephone +39 06 5635801, answered daily 09.00 to 17.30; the Ministero della cultura lists +39 06 56358099.
places.history: The park's own account takes the town's name from ostium, mouth, and records the tradition that Ancus Marcius founded it in 620 BC to work the salt pans, while the remains identified on the ground begin with the tufa-block castrum of the second half of the fourth century BC. Walls of about the middle of the first century BC enclosed roughly sixty-nine hectares behind three gates; population estimates for the second century AD run to around fifty thousand; commerce moved to Portus from the middle of the third century AD and literary sources describe the town abandoned by the middle of the sixth. The Tiber ran along the north side of the town until the flood of 1557, and the coastline is now about four kilometres away. The park is an autonomous institute of the Ministero della cultura created on 23 January 2016, directed by Alessandro D'Alessio since 30 October 2020, and it also administers sites in the Comune di Fiumicino. A birdwatching hide, Aves ostienses, stands on via della Foce inside the excavation under a three-year agreement with LIPU, which manages the hide and the neighbouring Casetta del Custode n. 4 and runs bird censuses on the site.

places.name: Museo Ostiense
places.summary: The state museum of the excavations, in the Casone del Sale inside the fenced area. The operator gives it as open Tuesday to Sunday, from 09.30 between 1 April and 24 October and from 10.30 between 25 October and 31 March, and always closed on the free first Sunday of the month and on the other ministry free days, 25 April, 2 June and 4 November. The finds are shown in twelve rooms on seven themes: the origins and the republican age, imperial power, civic spaces, the people, religions and cults, the necropoleis, and ways of living.
places.history: The building is a sixteenth-century structure tied to the papal salt monopoly and known as the Casone del Sale from the fifteenth century. It was restored between 1865 and 1867 for Pius IX to serve as a museum, which is when the neoclassical facade was built; the Ostian collections had been displayed in the Castello di Giulio II until the 1930s. The museum was inaugurated on 2 November 1934 under the excavation director Guido Calza, extended in part in 1952 and redisplayed in 1962. Among the named exhibits are the Vittoria Alata from the attic of Porta Romana, the statue of Cartilio Poplicola, fragments of the Fasti Ostienses, the Mithras Tauroctonos from the Mitreo delle Terme del Mitra signed by the Athenian artist Kriton, the statue of Trajan from the Schola del Traiano, the herm of Themistocles, the statue of Iulia Procula and the Sarcofago delle Muse.

places.name: Teatro romano di Ostia
places.summary: The town's theatre, on the Decumano Massimo inside the excavations, still used for performance. The Teatro di Roma runs the Teatro Ostia antica Festival - Il senso del passato here; its second edition runs from 25 June to 18 July 2026 with four productions, by Terzopoulos, Peltekis, Preljocaj and Dini.
places.history: Built in the last years of the first century BC and attested by an inscription naming Agrippa, then enlarged at the end of the second century AD to hold four thousand spectators. An arch in honour of Caracalla was thrown across the Decumanus at the entrance in 216 AD. A marble parapet was built later to isolate the cavea from the orchestra during water shows.

places.name: Piazzale delle Corporazioni
places.summary: The porticoed square behind the theatre, its floor paved with black-and-white mosaics carrying trading motifs and inscriptions that name Ostian and foreign guilds of merchants and shipowners.
places.history: Laid out with the theatre in the Augustan age and given its porticoes only under Claudius, in the middle of the first century AD. A temple on a high podium with two Corinthian columns was raised at the centre towards the end of the first century AD; the panel records that its dedicatee is not identified. The portico was doubled and the first mosaics laid in the first half of the second century AD, and they were remade later as the space was divided into stationes.

places.name: Grandi Horrea
places.summary: A grain warehouse of the excavated town, built round a colonnaded tufa courtyard with storage cellae on three sides.
places.history: Traditionally dated to the reign of Claudius, between 41 and 54 AD, with recent work proposing a first phase in the first century BC. It was rebuilt entirely in brick between the end of the second and the start of the third century AD, when two further rows of cellae were added in the courtyard, a first floor was built, and the floors were raised on suspensurae to keep the grain dry.

places.name: Horrea Epagathiana et Epaphroditiana
places.summary: A brick warehouse of about the middle of the second century AD, with a yellow-and-red brick portal, a mosaic-paved colonnaded court, sixteen rooms and at least two storeys.
places.history: The surviving inscription over the doorway names the owners Epagathus and Epaphroditus, probably two freedmen of Greek origin. Two aediculae in the court held statuettes of Fortuna and Venus. The double entrance door has been read as evidence that the building stored goods of value.

places.name: Foro di Ostia
places.summary: The main square of the excavated town, at the crossing of the Cardo Massimo and the Decumano Massimo in the middle of the old castrum: long, narrow and flanked by porticoes, with the Capitolium at the north end and the temple of Rome and Augustus facing it from the south.
places.history: The forum was laid out under Augustus and transformed under Hadrian. The temple of Rome and Augustus on the south side, in axis with the Capitolium, may have been built while Augustus was still alive, in the early first century AD; its substructures survive together with marble architectural elements, including the rear pediment and a flying Victory, re-mounted on a modern wall beside the building.

places.name: Capitolium di Ostia
places.summary: The temple of the Capitoline triad, on the north side of the Forum and in axis with the temple of Rome and Augustus at the other end of it.
places.history: Raised under Hadrian, about 120 AD, over an earlier cult building of the first century BC.

places.name: Basilica di Ostia
places.summary: The town's civil basilica, the hall used for justice and business, with a monumental entrance from the Decumanus and the judges' podium still visible at the far end.
places.history: Built between the end of the first and the start of the second century AD, with marble columns and a marble floor, and linked to the Forum by a double portico carrying a frieze of cupids and festoons.

places.name: Tempio di Ercole e area sacra repubblicana
places.summary: A republican temple on a high podium with a six-column pronaos, standing in a walled precinct that also holds the Tempio tetrastilo, the Aula delle Are and the Tempio dell'Ara rotonda. A copy of the votive statue of Cartilio Poplicola stands in the pronaos.
places.history: Raised between the end of the second and the start of the first century BC, with restorations documented into the fourth century AD. A marble relief dedicated by a haruspex shows a statue of Hercules recovered from the sea and a scene of divination. The remains were identified in 1794.

places.name: Terme del Foro di Ostia
places.summary: The public baths beside the Forum, with an octagonal heliocaminus, a laconicum and a suite of warm and hot rooms all turned south for the sun. The latrine and the palestra beside them are part of the same complex.
places.history: Built about 160 AD by Marco Gavio Massimo, praetorian prefect of Antoninus Pius. The building was remodelled substantially in the fourth and fifth centuries, when a monumental entrance was opened on Via della Forica.

places.name: Terme di Nettuno
places.summary: Baths on the Decumanus with two rooms of figured mosaics, a vaulted frigidarium with basins and a mosaic floor, two tepidaria, a calidarium and a colonnaded palestra on the west side. Flats with their own entrances occupied the upper floors.
places.history: Created at the end of the first century AD, rebuilt by Hadrian between 117 and 138 and completed in 139 AD by Antoninus Pius. Restoration work is documented into the fourth century AD.

places.name: Terme dei Sette Sapienti
places.summary: Baths in the residential quarter of the excavated town, named from a painting of the Seven Sages in a room that was probably a tavern before the baths absorbed it as a changing room.
places.history: Probably built under Hadrian, between 117 and 138 AD. The circular domed frigidarium keeps a hunting mosaic, and a second frigidarium keeps a painted Venus Anadyomene of the early third century AD.

places.name: Casa di Diana
places.summary: An apartment block on Via di Diana, perhaps five storeys when it was built, with shops along the street front and a porticoed courtyard at the centre.
places.history: Built under Hadrian, in the first half of the second century AD. Black-and-white geometric mosaics survive from the first phase; a marble fountain was added to the courtyard in the second half of the second century and the surviving wall paintings date from the end of it. The floors were raised and re-mosaiced through the third century, and a mithraeum was installed in the inner rooms in the late phase.

places.name: Thermopolium di Via di Diana
places.summary: A Roman bar on Via di Diana, with a marble serving counter, shelves, washing basins and still-life paintings above the shelves advertising what was served. Behind it is a courtyard with a small fountain and masonry benches for eating outside.
places.history: Carved in the third century AD out of a Hadrianic block. Three entrances open on the street, with seats under segmental-arched balconies carried on corbels, and the kitchen has a dolium sunk in the floor to keep food cool.

places.name: Case a Giardino
places.summary: A planned housing development of an outer quadrilateral and two symmetrical central blocks, separated by a garden with six fountains. External stairs led to the upper flats, which were generally let.
places.history: Built about 130 AD in a single operation, rising at least three storeys.

places.name: Domus di Amore e Psiche
places.summary: A late Roman house of two storeys, with an arcaded corridor opening on a garden and a marble nymphaeum along one side. The main hall keeps polychrome marble inlay on walls and floor.
places.history: Built in the fourth century AD over an earlier commercial building. A room off the corridor held the group of Cupid and Psyche that gives the house its name; a cast stands in its place and the original is in the Museo Ostiense.

places.name: Domus della Fortuna Annonaria
places.summary: An aristocratic house entered through a columned protiro and a vestibule, with a courtyard holding the cast of a female statue identified either as Fortuna Annonaria or as the personification of Ostia.
places.history: The present form is of the fourth century AD, built over a house of the middle of the second century whose peristyle it kept. The apsed main hall was built for a semicircular stibadium, and a private room was later converted into a heated hall with a mythological mosaic.

places.name: Caserma dei Vigili
places.summary: The barracks of the fire brigade, built round a porticoed courtyard with fountain troughs and rising at least two storeys. A chapel of the imperial cult stands on the far side of the courtyard and a corner latrine keeps an aedicula of Fortuna.
places.history: Built at the end of the first century AD, when a standing cohort of vigiles was stationed at Ostia; the layout visible now is the Hadrianic rebuild, and the chapel was monumentalised in the early third century AD.

places.name: Serapeo di Ostia
places.summary: The temple of Serapis, standing on a podium behind a four-column pronaos with coloured marble paving, in a porticoed court with a central altar and a Nilotic mosaic. The inscription IOVI SERAPI is kept in the courtyard.
places.history: Built at the expense of the freedman Caltilius and inaugurated on 24 January 127 AD, Hadrian's birthday. The colonnaded entrance was added later in the second century and paved with a mosaic of the Apis bull.

places.name: Mitreo di Felicissimo
places.summary: A mithraeum whose mosaic floor carries a krater, a flaming altar and two Phrygian caps, with a corridor mosaic of seven panels alluding to the grades of initiation and the planets attached to them.
places.history: Installed in the second half of the third century AD inside an earlier building. An eighth panel carries the inscription naming Felicissimus, who built it.

places.name: Sinagoga di Ostia
places.summary: The synagogue of the Ostian Jewish community: a vestibule, a colonnaded entrance, and a prayer hall with a raised bimah at the far end oriented towards Jerusalem. An aedicula for the Torah scrolls is surmounted by corbels carved with the seven-branched menorah.
places.history: Built about the middle of the first century AD for the local Jewish community and rebuilt completely in the fourth century AD. A large adjoining hall has benches, and a room with an oven and a counter has been read as a place to make unleavened bread.

places.name: Campo della Magna Mater
places.summary: A triangular sanctuary precinct in the angle between the Cardo Massimo and the town walls, holding the temple of Cybele, the shrine of Attis, the temple of Bellona and the seat of the hastiferi. The taurobolia were performed in the open ground between them.
places.history: The cult of Cybele reached Ostia in the first century AD and the sanctuary was laid out during the second.

places.name: Mura repubblicane e Porta Romana
places.summary: The town wall and the gate that carried the road from Rome into it. Porta Romana had two bays and keeps part of its marble facing; of the two Minerva-Victory statues that flanked it, one original is in the Museo Ostiense and a copy stands in the piazzale.
places.history: The walls were built about the middle of the first century BC on three sides of the town, enclosing about sixty-nine hectares behind three gates flanked by square towers. The inscription from the attic, recorded on both faces, states that the Senate and People of Rome decreed the walls of the Ostian colony, that Marcus Tullius Cicero began the work and let the contract, and that Publius Clodius Pulcher, tribune of the plebs, completed and approved it.

places.name: Castrum repubblicano di Ostia
places.summary: The fortified rectangular nucleus the town grew out of, its tufa-block walls traceable inside the later street plan, with four gates at the ends of the cardo and the decumanus.
places.history: Dated to the fourth century BC. Its cardo and decumanus set the axes the later town kept, and they cross at the Forum.

places.name: Necropoli della via Ostiense
places.summary: The tomb road outside Porta Romana, on Via delle Tombe. Two of its monuments carry their own panels: the Tomba degli Archetti and the Colombari gemelli.
places.history: The Tomba degli Archetti was built at the start of the first century AD as a funerary enclosure in reticulate work; its north facade carries brick architectural members under arches, with the lunettes inlaid in yellow and red brick alternating with tufa and pumice. It was converted into a columbarium in the second half of the first century AD, and larger arcosolia were added from the second. The Colombari gemelli are two independent tombs of the first half of the first century AD built to the same plan, each with an open vestibule and a covered chamber of urn niches, and terrace roofs reached by stairs for funerary banquets; the ustrinum lay in the space between them.

places.name: Necropoli Laurentina
places.summary: One of the two burial grounds of the ancient town inside the archaeological park. The operator states that it is closed to the public for maintenance and restoration work.
places.history: Excavated from 1804 and then sporadically through the nineteenth century. The four painted tombs found in 1865 are known as the Tombe dei Claudii, and their detached paintings are in the Musei Vaticani. Excavation resumed in 1934 and brought up about fifty burials. Tomb 18, the Sacerdotessa Isiaca, holds an Augustan stucco cycle, and tomb 32, Orfeo agli inferi, a well preserved painted cycle of birds and fruit on yellow and red grounds.

places.name: Castello di Giulio II
places.summary: The triangular brick fortress on Piazza della Rocca, with three corner towers joined by a single wall-walk, a perimeter of casemates, a rivellino and a wide moat once fed from the Tiber. The operator gives it as open Tuesday to Sunday, 10.30 to 16.30 from 1 November to the end of February, 10.30 to 19.30 from 1 March to 15 June and 13.30 to 19.30 from 16 June to 31 October, with last entry thirty minutes before closing; closed Mondays, 25 December and 1 January. Admission is 6.00 euro full and 2.00 euro reduced for EU citizens aged 18 to 25, and it is covered by the 18.00 euro integrated ticket. Restoration, consolidation and enhancement works are under way, and the operator states that the castle stays open on its usual hours during them, with panels explaining the work. The exhibition IN HOC SIGNO. Testimonianze cristiane tra Ostia e Porto runs until 21 November 2026.
places.history: Work began in 1483 at the expense of Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere, later Julius II, and was completed in 1486. Roma Capitale records that the inscription on the courtyard portal names the Florentine architect Baccio Pontelli; Vasari attributed the design to Giuliano da Sangallo, and other historians have proposed Francesco di Giorgio Martini. The fortress absorbed the tower Martin V had built, dated by it.wikipedia to 1423 and 1424, which is the larger, many-sided one of its three corner towers; the other two are round. The walls are brick, low, thick and battered. The monumental staircase was frescoed with the myth of Hercules, attributed to Baldassarre Peruzzi. The castle's customs role passed to Tor Boacciana in 1562 and then to Tor San Michele in 1568, and it.wikipedia records that the building was used in the nineteenth century as a prison for convicts sentenced to forced labour.

places.name: Borgo di Ostia Antica (Gregoriopoli)
places.summary: The walled village around the castle on Piazza della Rocca, facing the archaeological area across viale dei Romagnoli. Three rows of terraced houses built inside the walls in the fifteenth century are still lived in.
places.history: From late antiquity the area held the Christian community's cemetery, on the site where tradition placed the tombs of martyrs, among them Santa Aurea. Pope Gregory IV, who reigned from 827 to 844, turned the settlement into a fortified citadel and named it Gregoriopoli. Martin V had a round tower with a moat built to watch the Tiber, dated by it.wikipedia to 1423 and 1424. Cardinal Guillaume d'Estouteville, bishop of Ostia from 1461 to 1483, restored the Gregoriopoli walls and built the three rows of terraced houses inside them. The siege by the Duke of Alba in 1556 and the flood of 1557, which diverted the Tiber, emptied the borgo, and malarial marshes followed. The rocca and the borgo were restored in stages during the twentieth century.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Aurea
places.summary: The cathedral of the suburbicarian diocese of Ostia, on Piazza della Rocca beside the castle. It has a single nave with a trussed ceiling, lit by a rose window and fifteenth-century mullioned windows. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The church is first mentioned in connection with restorations ordered by Pope Sergius II in the middle of the eighth century. The present building was begun at the wish of Cardinal Guillaume d'Estouteville, completed under Giuliano della Rovere and finished in 1483; the parish names Baccio Pontelli as its architect, the same man named for the fortress next to it, and he reversed the church's orientation. The chapel of Santa Monica on the right holds a funerary inscription found near the church in 1945 that records the ancient cult of the saint's body, and a canvas of the Ecstasy of Saint Monica attributed to Pietro da Cortona; the oval Martirio di santa Aurea among the seventeenth-century altarpieces is given to Andrea Sacchi. The apse arch is built of spoliated marble and carries sixteenth-century frescoes, and the modern altar carries two fifteenth-century reliefs. The see has been entrusted since 1966 to the vicar of the diocese of Rome, its cardinalatial title has been held since the twelfth century by the Dean of the College of Cardinals, and twelve bishops of Ostia have been elected pope.

places.name: Area archeologico-naturalistica delle Saline
places.summary: The remains of Ostia's river harbour, outside the fenced excavation and reached from viale dei Romagnoli by via delle Saline. The quay is a tufa-block revetment more than 100 metres long and 15 metres wide, its western end shaped as a mole head, with reticulate-work walls set at right angles linking the quay to the shore. The area is almost entirely reburied. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: The structure is known as the molo repubblicano, though the operator states that the republican dating cannot be taken as certain.

places.name: Parco dei Ravennati
places.summary: A public park in the borgo, lying between via dei Martiri Ostiensi, via della Gente Salinatoria, via del Mare, viale dei Romagnoli, via Gesualdo and via Gloriano. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: It is dedicated to the men who drained the marshes at Ostia.

entries.name: Parco archeologico di Ostia antica
entries.note: One ticket office at Viale dei Romagnoli 717 opens the whole excavation: 18.00 euro full, 2.00 euro reduced, valid eight consecutive days across all the institute's sites.

entries.name: Teatro romano di Ostia
entries.note: Built in the last years of the first century BC and enlarged at the end of the second century AD to hold four thousand, it still stages a summer festival run by the Teatro di Roma.

entries.name: Piazzale delle Corporazioni
entries.note: The mosaics of this porticoed square behind the theatre carry trading motifs and inscriptions naming Ostian and foreign guilds of merchants and shipowners.

entries.name: Thermopolium di Via di Diana
entries.note: A Roman bar carved out of a Hadrianic block in the third century AD, with its marble counter, its washing basins and paintings above the shelves advertising what was served.

entries.name: Casa di Diana
entries.note: A Hadrianic apartment block on Via di Diana, perhaps five storeys when new, with shops on the street, a porticoed courtyard and a mithraeum installed in its inner rooms late on.

entries.name: Terme di Nettuno
entries.note: Baths begun at the end of the first century AD, rebuilt by Hadrian and completed in 139 AD by Antoninus Pius, with figured mosaics and a colonnaded palestra.

entries.name: Sinagoga di Ostia
entries.note: Built about the middle of the first century AD and rebuilt in the fourth, with a bimah oriented towards Jerusalem and corbels carved with the seven-branched menorah.

entries.name: Mura repubblicane e Porta Romana
entries.note: The attic inscription of the gate records that Cicero began the walls of the Ostian colony and let the contract, and that Clodius Pulcher completed and approved the work.

entries.name: Museo Ostiense
entries.note: The finds are shown in twelve rooms on seven themes inside the Casone del Sale, a salt store restored for Pius IX and opened as a museum on 2 November 1934.

entries.name: Necropoli Laurentina
entries.note: Do not plan on this one: the operator states that the necropolis is closed to the public for maintenance and restoration work.

entries.name: Castello di Giulio II
entries.note: Begun in 1483 for Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere and completed in 1486, with a staircase frescoed with the myth of Hercules attributed to Baldassarre Peruzzi.

entries.name: Borgo di Ostia Antica
entries.note: Gregory IV made a fortified citadel of the settlement in the ninth century, and the three rows of terraced houses d'Estouteville built inside its walls are still lived in.

entries.name: Basilica di Sant'Aurea
entries.note: The cathedral of the diocese of Ostia, finished in 1483 by the architect of the fortress beside it, with an oval Martirio di santa Aurea given to Andrea Sacchi.
